plants.name: Camellia japonica
plants.description: An evergreen shrub with glossy dark green leaves and rose-like flowers. It thrives in mild, humid climates and is a mainstay of winter gardens, with thousands of cultivars in varied forms.
plants.bloomingSeason: Late autumn through early spring, peaking in mid-winter
plants.location: Native to Japan, Korea and China; widely cultivated in the southeastern United States, Western Europe, and Australia
plants.funFact: Camellia sinensis, a close relative, is the plant from which all true tea is made.

plants.name: Helleborus niger
plants.description: A low-growing perennial with nodding, cup-shaped white flowers with golden stamens that often fade to pink. It flowers in cold weather and tolerates frost and snow.
plants.location: Native to the mountains of central and southern Europe; cultivated in temperate gardens in Europe and North America
plants.funFact: Despite its name, it is not a true rose but a member of the buttercup family, and all parts are toxic.

plants.name: Protea cynaroides
plants.description: A shrub bearing the largest flower head in the Protea genus, a massive bowl-shaped bloom of pointed bracts surrounding a central cluster of florets. It is adapted to nutrient-poor soils and fire-prone fynbos.
plants.bloomingSeason: Southern Hemisphere late spring to summer, with flowering often continuing into January
plants.location: Native to the fynbos of South Africa's Western and Eastern Cape; cultivated in Australia, California, and Hawaii
plants.funFact: It is the national flower of South Africa, and its flower heads can reach 30 cm across.

plants.name: Hamamelis mollis
plants.description: A deciduous shrub that produces spidery, strongly fragrant flowers on bare branches in winter. The ribbon-like petals curl up in cold weather and unfurl again when it warms.
plants.location: Native to central and eastern China; grown in temperate gardens in Europe, North America, and Japan
plants.funFact: Witch hazel flowers can survive freezing temperatures by curling their petals tightly to protect themselves.
